summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people or consensual same-sex conduct. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1971, the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1999, homosexuality was declassified as an illness in 1981 and transvestism in 2011. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation became a criminal offence in 1995 and discrimination on grounds of gender identity in 2005.

Section 8(1) of the Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and other personal characteristics, whether the treatment rests on fact or assumption; gender identity and expression have been covered since 2005. The Act on Equality between Women and Men covers sex and gender identity, and a 2014 parliamentary amendment extended its protections to employment, goods and services, education and health services.

Legal gender recognition was reformed in 2023. The age limit is 18, down from a proposal that would have allowed the change at 15 with guardian permission; applicants face a 30-day reflection period and may change legal gender once per year. Until April 2023 an applicant had to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and hold a mental disorder diagnosis.

Finland was one of three countries that wrote an infertility requirement into its statute for legal gender recognition. An investigation published on 10 September 2025 recorded at least 11,000 people subjected to such conditions across the six countries examined, and the last requirement in that group was phased out at the end of June 2025. Finland's own statutory requirement ended with the 2023 reform, leaving a documented cohort of people who lived under it.

Police recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences in the latest reporting year, the highest figure ever recorded, with defamation and assault the most common types. Sexual orientation and gender identity were recurrent motives, accounting for 12% of cases, and the sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category rose across six reported years from 72 to 241. The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence, so motive is captured only in police reports and these incidents are counted as reported suspicion rather than as charges.

Finland's first conversion-practices prosecution ended in convictions in March, brought as assault. Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices by 125 votes to 49 in March, while a full statutory ban remained pending at the close of the review period.

Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units. A Seta survey found over 40% of trans respondents entirely unable to access the care they needed, most of them reporting extended waiting times.

Clinical recommendations for gender dysphoria under age 25, revised in 2020 by the Council for Choices in Health Care, prioritise psychosocial therapy over medical transition and restrict puberty blockers and hormone treatment. They are recommendations rather than mandates: puberty blockers remain available case by case, and cross-sex hormones can be considered where the identity is of a permanent nature causing severe dysphoria.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal on 1 March 2017. Registered partnerships, available from 2002 until that date, carried the rights of married couples except adoption and a joint surname, and gave immigration rights to a foreign same-sex partner. Stepchild adoption became legal in 2009. A 2018 amendment to the Maternity Act recognises both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of the child's birth, with second-parent registration fixed at birth rather than by adoption, and an April 2019 law passed 122-42 gave lesbian couples full maternity pay and parentage rights without intra-family adoption. Surrogacy remains illegal for all couples.
tangentialFactors:
Finland updated its travel advice for transgender citizens travelling to the United States in March 2025, after reports of border difficulties following a US executive order recognising only two genders. The advice is outbound guidance issued to Finland's own travellers and is not an assessment of risk within Finland.

Finnish police reported 73 violent attacks and assaults against LGBT people in 2018, a 27% increase on 2017 and the only hate-motive category to rise that year. The figure covers LGBT people generally, with no trans breakdown and no population denominator, and no later comparable figure appears in this record.

In November 2019 the Institute of Health and Welfare reported that LGBT children and youth face significantly more bullying, physical, psychological and sexual violence than heterosexual peers, and are more likely to suffer violence at home.

The citizens' initiative route is a live legislative channel: 50,000 valid signatures oblige Parliament to consider a proposal, and the 2013 marriage initiative drew more than 162,000 certified signatures before Parliament approved the change by 101-90 in December 2014. The same route produced the conversion-practices initiative endorsed in March.

Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden are the three countries identified as having written infertility requirements into law for legal gender recognition.

People sterilised or made infertile under the previous requirement, and those who held a mental disorder diagnosis as a condition of recognition, form a documented legacy cohort.

Seta's survey of trans respondents records over 40% unable to access the care they needed, most citing extended waiting times.

The Act on Equality between Women and Men, as amended in 2014, extends to employment, goods and services, education and health services.

Because the Criminal Code has no hate-crime offence, residents reporting a bias incident have their motive recorded in police files rather than charged as a distinct offence; the national total of 1,808 suspected hate crimes reflects reported suspicion.

Conversion practices were prosecuted for the first time, as assault, with convictions in March, and Parliament endorsed a ban by 125-49 in March while the statutory prohibition remained pending.

Support organisations operate nationwide: Seta, founded in 1974, Trasek for trans and intersex rights, and Rainbow Families.
outOfScopeNotes:
The two sources date the figure of 1,808 suspected hate crimes differently: the Police University College release of November 2025 assigns it to 2024, while the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 assigns it to 2025 with a 13% rise since 2023. This discrepancy is unresolved in the record.

The Seta survey reporting over 40% of trans respondents unable to access needed care does not state its fieldwork period, so the currency of that figure is unresolved.

The violence figures in this record are LGBT-wide, without a trans-specific breakdown, a period-matched general homicide rate or a population denominator, so they cannot be read as a trans-specific rate.

The status of the conversion-practices statutory ban after Parliament's March endorsement is unresolved; the record shows endorsement, not enactment.

No entry, visa or border-screening treatment specific to trans travellers arriving in Finland is documented in this inventory.
